description: Host memory (RAM) of an Idol session built and run in staged mode, whose waiting models sit in memory, compared with lean mode, whose waiting models sit in files on disk (tools/idol_lowram.py). Also the speed of restoring a model from disk, and what remains when everything is on disk.
machine: Windows 11 Home, 64 GiB RAM (about 22 GiB free), NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 (24,564 MiB), PyTorch 2.10.0+cu128. The graphics device was shared throughout with an unrelated workload at 100% utilization using 16 to 20 GiB, so every elapsed time here is contaminated; memory figures are not affected by that.

inputs.encoders: original DINOv3 and FLUX.2 autoencoder, bfloat16
inputs.note: Two denoising steps instead of 50 keep each run short; host memory does not depend on the step count, but the point cloud compared below is a two-step result.

metric.name: private working set
metric.definition: Pages resident in the process that are not file-backed or shareable (the Windows Task Manager 'Memory' column), read from QueryWorkingSet every 200 ms, so a shorter peak can be missed. The process working set (RSS) also counts memory-mapped model files and PyTorch's mapped libraries, which the system can drop and read again; it was 7,799 to 7,918 MiB in staged mode and 5,494 to 7,907 MiB in lean mode, and is not the memory that must fit.
metric.phases: Peaks are labelled by the last pipeline checkpoint passed: 'checkpoint 1' to '3' are the denoiser, background remover and image encoders being built, 'checkpoint 5' the decoders, 'checkpoint 6' onward one generation.

peaks_mib.note: Two runs of each, in the order given; the pairs agree within 0.3%. The thresholds in tools/idol_memory.py use the larger value.

output.result: The point cloud (17,826,208 bytes, SHA-256 528eddebadb2b446332be0fca994faf2fcf10129bb551a3789b5841f07813bce) was byte-identical in 2 staged runs and 5 lean runs, including runs before and after the faster reader below.
output.limit: One image, one seed, two steps.

floor.description: Private working set at steps of a lean session, in MiB (two separate processes).
floor.reading: Nothing in the process accounts for the memory above the 674 MiB of a bare PyTorch and CUDA process: no CPU tensor of any size was alive after a generation (6 tiny storages), and closing the session and deleting the cache did not lower it. A walk of the address space after the build found 3,724 MiB committed in private regions, 1,057 MiB of it in regions of 64 to 128 MiB and 1,961 MiB in regions of 16 to 64 MiB, which is the pattern of driver and allocator reservations; committed is not resident, and no further attribution was made. This is why lean mode stops at about 3.3 GB: the remaining memory is held by PyTorch, CUDA and the graphics driver, not by the models.

restore.description: Reading the real lean cache files back, best of two repeats, into buffers of the stored types. The graphics device was busy with another workload, which slows copies to it.
restore.per_model_note: [safetensors, in order]. Sizes in MiB as stored: denoiser 741, background remover 844 (stored in full precision; the session runs it in half precision, so a real restore converts it), image encoders 1,603, image autoencoder 160, octree decoder 113, Gaussian decoder 241.

single_buffered_reader_device_seconds.note: An earlier run with one buffer, while the device was busier.

restore.many_small_tensors: On a synthetic model of 1,560 tensors (492 MiB) get_tensor ran at 72 to 84 MiB/s and the in-order reader at 929 to 1,042 MiB/s, because get_tensor costs milliseconds per tensor on Windows. On 250 large tensors (1,600 MiB) the in-order reader was 1.4 to 1.5 times faster.

elapsed_seconds_unreliable.note: The pairs disagree in sign because the graphics device was shared with another workload; they are not a measurement of lean mode's cost. A generation in lean mode restores about 3.7 GB, which took 3.5 s in the restore measurement above.

not_established: A run on a real computer with little memory. The Windows figures are of the process on a 64 GiB computer, where the system does not take memory back from it; the container test above limits the process but not an operating system beside it.
The operating system's own use, which is why the thresholds add a 1,024 MiB headroom.
Linux or macOS; the metric is a Windows one.

Host memory of the separate image generator was measured afterwards (text-prompt-host-memory.json): it needs about 6.8 GB of private host memory at graphics budgets of 4 GiB and below, so a text prompt needs more host memory than Idol in lean mode does unless the generator's weights are memory-mapped, which the server now chooses when the system memory is short (3.8 GB private for a whole request in lean mode with mapping, same point cloud).

capped_container.description: The server's Runtime (tools/idol_server.py, default probes) building a session and generating twice inside a Linux container with a hard memory limit and no swap, to test the one thing the Windows figures cannot: whether the process survives a small memory limit.
capped_container.method: docker run --gpus all --memory=N --memory-swap=N (cgroup v2, Docker Desktop on WSL2, container image built from commit 98bf745), the model and the Hugging Face cache mounted read-only, HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1, Runtime(vram_budget_gib=4) so that the graphics plan is staged, and --memory-mode auto, staged or lean. Counters are the container's own (memory.stat, memory.events), sampled every 100 ms, so a shorter peak can be missed. 'anon' is the process's own memory; 'file' is page cache, which the kernel drops and reads again, and which fills the limit by design. Two generations of the axolotl image, seed 42, two steps, original encoders.

runs.mode: auto (chose lean because the cgroup limit left 6,128 MiB free, under the 6,207 MiB threshold)

runs.result: killed for running out of memory during the second generation
killed for running out of memory before the first generation finished (38 s in)

capped_container.reading: Under a hard 4 GiB limit lean mode finished two generations and staged mode did not finish one; under 6 GiB lean mode finished and staged mode was killed in its second generation. The lean output was identical across the two limits and across the two generations. The process's own memory peaked at about 2.3 GB, below the 3.3 GB measured on Windows, because the Windows figure includes pages the driver and libraries hold that Linux counts elsewhere; the thresholds in tools/idol_memory.py use the Windows figures and are therefore conservative on Linux.
not_shown: A real 4 GB computer. The limit applies to this process alone; an operating system, a desktop and other programs beside it are not counted, which is the reason the thresholds add 1,024 MiB.

The graphics side of a 4 GB card. The device was a 24 GB card with another workload on it, and the 4 GiB was a stated budget; the staged process's measured graphics peak (2,754 MiB, docs/data/idol-staged-memory.json) is what suggests it fits.
That lean and staged outputs are identical on Linux: staged mode was killed before it wrote its second result, and its first result was not hashed. Their equality was shown on Windows.
Speed. Both the graphics device and the Windows file-sharing layer under the mounted files were busy, and the first generation includes building the session.
